latin.76: III. Ex verf. 16. sic ratiocinatur. Hic κρίμα, judicium sive reatus ex Adamo, opponitur δώρημα Christi. Ergo ut δώρημα non significat qualitatem aliquam nobis inherentem, sed quod in Christo est, & in Christo nobis gratis imputatur; Ita κρίμα aliquid significare debet, quod sit extra nos, nempe culpam ab Adamo patratam, unde reatum & condemnationem trahimus. Collige. Cujus culpa est in omnium condemnationem, eam omnibus imputari oportet. Atqui culpa Adami est in omnium condemnationem. Ergo eam omnibus imputari oportet.
latin.77: Nihil roboris in hoc argumento video, quod non extet in superioribus jam abundè refutatis. Quae enim & quam imbecilla est haec collectio; Hic κρίμα judicium sive reatus ex Adamo, opponitur δώρημα Christi. Ergo ut hoc non significat qualitatem nobis inhaerentem, sic nec illud?
latin.78: Quid enim prohibet, vitium inhaerens quatenus nos facit reos & poena dignos ei justitiae opponi, quae nos ab eo reatu & poena liberat, uti vidimus censuisse maximos viros? Id non modo nihil prohibet, sed ipsa illa oppositio exigit. Est enim κρίμα ex justitia, δώρημα ex gratia. Justitia nonnisi suum cuique tribuit; gratia donat id quod alioqui nostrum non erat, sed alienum.
latin.79: Hoc accepi a Chamiero, Si nihil, inquit, habent infantes peccati proprii, cur propria morte pereunt? Nam propter alienam culpam, quae tantum aliena sit, non fert justitia divina. Habuerint sane aliquando homines eum morem, ut patris servitus, filiis esset hereditaria: at ejusmodi nihil erat in populo Dei, ex divinis legibus: quanto minus in Deo: qui irascitur in eos, quibus erat in ore proverbium, Patres nostri uvas acerbas comederunt: Filiis autem dentes stupent;
latin.80: Quod si excipiat quis, servari fideles propter justitiam non suam, sed Christi: itaque posse etiam damnari, propter alienam injustitiam, is vero non videt comparari valde diversa. Nam damnatio est a justitia, salus autem a gratia. Nam si esset etiam ipsa a justitia, non posset nos aliena justitia servare: quare ne aliena quidem culpa damnare. Nihil, opinor, desiderari potuit disertius.

pass_a.76: Garissoles's third argument starts from Romans 5:16. He says the Apostle sets Adam's κρίμα (the judgment or the guilt-verdict that comes from Adam) over against Christ's δώρημα. From that opposition he infers: δώρημα does not name a quality that lives in us; it names what stands in Christ and is freely counted to us in Christ. Therefore κρίμα likewise must name something outside us — the very fault Adam committed — and from that outside fault we pull guilt and condemnation. The collected syllogism: whatever fault runs out into the condemnation of all must be imputed to all; Adam's fault does so run; therefore Adam's fault must be imputed to all.
pass_a.77: Placeus answers that this argument has no muscle that was not already in the earlier opposition-arguments, and those have been refuted at length. He asks how thin the collection is: because κρίμα (judgment / guilt from Adam) is set opposite Christ's δώρημα, does it follow that, since the gift does not mean an inhering quality, the κρίμα also cannot mean one?
pass_a.78: What blocks us from setting an inhering vice — taken as what makes us guilty and fit for penalty — opposite the justice that releases us from that guilt and penalty? The greatest writers, Placeus notes, have already judged that way. Nothing blocks it; the opposition itself presses for it. κρίμα comes out of justice; δώρημα comes out of grace. Justice pays each person only what is already his; grace hands over what was not ours before, but someone else's.
pass_a.79: Placeus says he took the next stroke from Chamier. Chamier asks: if infants have no sin of their own, why do they die a death that is their own? Divine justice will not carry a fault that is merely someone else's. Human law may once have made a father's slavery pass to the sons as inheritance; nothing like that stood among God's people under the divine statutes — and still less in God himself, who grows angry at the people who kept saying the proverb about fathers eating sour grapes and children's teeth going dull.
pass_a.80: Suppose someone replies that believers are saved by a righteousness that is not theirs but Christ's, and so they could also be damned by an injustice that is not theirs. Chamier (via Placeus) says that person fails to see how unlike the two cases are. Damnation comes from justice; salvation comes from grace. If salvation itself ran on justice, another person's righteousness could not save us; and on the same footing another person's guilt could not damn us. Placeus closes: nothing more plain could have been wanted.

76: III. From verse 16 he reasons thus. Here κρίμα, judgment or guilt from Adam, is set opposite Christ's δώρημα (Romans 5:16). Therefore, as δώρημα does not signify some quality inhering in us, but what is in Christ, and is freely imputed to us in Christ, so κρίμα must signify something outside us — namely the fault committed by Adam, from which we draw guilt and condemnation. Collect: Whose fault is unto the condemnation of all, that fault must be imputed to all. But Adam's fault is unto the condemnation of all. Therefore it must be imputed to all.
77: I see no strength in this argument that is not already present in the earlier ones, now amply refuted. For how weak this collection is: Here κρίμα, judgment or guilt from Adam, is set opposite Christ's δώρημα. Therefore, as the one does not signify a quality inhering in us, neither does the other?
78: For what forbids an inhering vice, insofar as it makes us guilty and worthy of penalty, from being set opposite that justice which frees us from that guilt and penalty — as we have seen the greatest men judged? Not only does nothing forbid it; that very opposition requires it. For κρίμα is from justice, δώρημα from grace. Justice assigns to each only what is his own; grace gives what was otherwise not ours, but another's.
79: I took this from Chamier. "If infants," he says, "have nothing of their own sin, why do they perish by their own death? For divine justice does not bear an alien fault that is only alien. Men may once have had the custom that a father's slavery was hereditary for the sons; but nothing of that kind stood in the people of God under the divine laws — how much less in God, who is angry at those who had in their mouth the proverb, Our fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge" (Ezekiel 18:2).
80: But if someone objects that the faithful are saved on account of a righteousness not their own but Christ's, and that therefore they can also be damned on account of an alien injustice, he truly does not see that very different things are being compared. For damnation is from justice, but salvation is from grace. For if salvation itself were also from justice, an alien righteousness could not save us; so neither can an alien guilt damn. Nothing, I think, could have been wanted more expressly.
